title: Chapter 9: Of Free Will - Westminster Confession of Faith
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: This lesson introduces a 13-part series on sanctification using Chapter 9 of the Westminster Confession of Faith on the freedom of the will. Pastor Lyro explains that human will is free to act according to our nature (heart), not bound by external forces, and examines the will's condition in five states: before the fall, after the fall, after regeneration, and in glory. The lesson emphasizes that liberty (freedom to choose) differs from ability (capacity to do), and concludes with practical applications including humility, dependence on God's grace, evangelistic prayer, and encouragement in spiritual struggle.

outline.title: Understanding the Nature of Human Will
subpoints: The will determines what a person will do based on understanding and natural inclination
The will is bound to our nature (heart), not to external forces
Liberty means freedom to act according to our nature; ability means capacity to change our preferences
Nature (heart) is what drives the will, not the will itself

outline.title: The Will Before the Fall (Paragraph 2)
subpoints: Adam had freedom and power to will and do good and what pleased God
His will was changeable (mutable), so he could fall from righteousness
He was able to sin and able not to sin (posse peccare, non posse non peccare)
The fall demonstrates the changeable nature of pre-fall humanity

outline.title: The Will After the Fall (Paragraph 3)
subpoints: Natural man has lost all ability to will spiritual good that accompanies salvation
The natural man is averse from good and dead in sin
Cannot convert himself or prepare himself for salvation through his own strength
The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit and cannot know them
The state is non posse peccare non peccare (not able not to sin)

outline.title: The Will After Regeneration (Paragraph 4)
subpoints: God frees the converted sinner from natural bondage under sin through grace alone
The regenerate person is enabled freely to will and do spiritual good
Remaining corruption means the believer still battles and chooses both good and evil
Spiritual struggle is evidence of the presence of the Holy Spirit
The state is posse peccare, non posse peccare (able to sin, able not to sin)

outline.title: The Will in Glory (Paragraph 5)
subpoints: In eternity, the will is made perfectly and immutably free to good alone
This is a greater state than Adam before the fall
We will not be able to sin in heaven
Believers will be like Christ and unable to sin
The state is non posse peccare (not able to sin)

outline.title: Practical Applications of the Doctrine
subpoints: Humility before God: we cannot boast in our conversion since salvation is entirely by grace
Complete dependence on God's grace rather than our own strength
Prayer for the salvation of unbelievers, knowing God changes hearts
Faithful evangelism without burden for results, trusting the Holy Spirit
Encouragement in spiritual struggle, recognizing conflict as evidence of spiritual life

transcript:
## Introduction to the Series

We are starting a new thirteen-part series today on the journey from regeneration all the way to glorification. There will be several of us teaching this series. We're going to use the Confession of Faith in chapter 9 to guide us through it.

## Building Progress Update

You can see the work continues on our building. They had left Thursday and left everything where it was, so we had to have them come back yesterday to reposition their stuff so we could have access to the parking lot. That's the waterline they're putting in right now. The city inspector came and approved it, so work continues.

## Opening the Westminster Confession of Faith

I would love for you to grab a hymnal and turn to the back part using the little numbers on the bottom of the page to page 854. That's where you're going to find chapter 9 of the Westminster Confession of Faith. Chapter 9 is called "Of Free Will." I'm going to read the whole chapter and then we're going to consider it as we go through this series.

### Westminster Confession of Faith, Chapter 9: Of Free Will

> God has endued the will of man with that natural liberty that is neither forced nor by any absolute necessity of nature determined to do good or evil. Man, in his state of innocence, had freedom and power to will and to do that which was good and well pleasing to God, but yet mutably, so that he might fall from it. Man, by his fall into a state of sin, has wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation. So as a natural man being altogether averse from that good and dead in sin is not able by his own strength to convert himself or to prepare himself there unto. When God converts a sinner and translates him into the state of grace, he frees him from his natural bondage under sin and by his grace alone enables him freely to will and to do that which is spiritually good. Yet so as that by reason of his remaining corruption, he does not perfectly nor only will that which is good, but does also will that which is evil. The will of man is made perfect and immutably free to good alone in the state of glory only.

## Understanding the Will

The will is that part of the human mind which determines what the person will do. It makes a decision from two bases. The first is the understanding of the situation—what you know about what's going on. The second is the will's reading of the person's natural inclination and priorities—the person's nature.

The point is that our will is really free and is not absolutely submitted to anything outside of ourselves. The only thing that our will is bound to is our nature, in the sense that we are not going to choose or act contrary to who we are.

### Nature Equals Heart

Another word for nature—the one that's used in the Bible the most—is heart. The heart is the way that the Bible speaks about our nature, of who we truly are, the core of our being.

The Lord Jesus speaks of this in Matthew 12:

> A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good. Out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. An evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings forth evil.

In Luke 6:45:

> A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings forth evil things.

In Proverbs 4:23:

> Keep your heart with all diligence for out of it springs all the issues of life.

Everything who we are, what we choose comes from our heart, not from anywhere else. We are not absolutely bound to anything outside of ourselves—only to our own heart as far as our will goes.

## Freedom of the Will Defined

When we say the will is free, we mean that the will is free to express a person's nature. The will is free to do what you want to do in your heart, to express who you are. We do not mean that the will is free to choose what is right, because the will is not forced to act contrary to the person's nature.

That's what we mean by free will: your will is free to act according to your nature. An insane person makes a decision unrelated to their nature and knowledge. But nature is stronger than knowledge. We make decisions contrary to what we know about Christ, even as redeemed people. That's what sin is—decisions contrary to who Christ is. And we're doing that with perfect knowledge that that's not what God wants us to do.

### The Problem People Have With This Doctrine

The problem that people have with this doctrine is that if the will is bound to our nature, and the natural man is sinful, then the will is not going to choose God. Some say this means we're not free. Others say that the Bible commands us to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, but you're saying we don't have the freedom to do that or the ability to do that.

This is a very important thing to distinguish. A. A. Hodge, in his book *Outlines of Theology*, defines liberty and ability:

Liberty consists in the power of the agent to will as he pleases from the fact that the volition is determined only by the character of the agent willing. We have complete freedom and liberty.

But liberty is not the same as ability. If Tim chooses to fly and climbs on the roof and steps on the tip of the steeple and chooses to fly, he's free to make that decision. But does he have the ability? Once he lets go, what happens? Liberty and ability are two distinct things. You can be free to choose something while not being able to do the thing that you choose to do.

Hodge defines ability as the power of the agent to change his own subjective state, to make himself prefer what he does not prefer, and to act in a given case in opposition to the coexistent desires and preferences of the agent's own heart.

Hodge concludes:

> Thus man is truly free since the fall as before it because he wills as his evil heart pleases. But he has lost all ability to obey the law of God because his evil heart is not subject to that law, neither can he change it.

Freedom and ability are two different things. We need to keep that in mind. You can choose between coconut ice cream and chocolate ice cream. You can choose between Coke Zero and that Coke. You can choose between kale and steak. But we're talking about moral choices when we talk about the will here. We're not addressing alternate choices between things that are good or neutral. We're specifically discussing moral choices.

## The Five Paragraphs: The Will Under Four Administrations

### Section One: The Will Is Free From Exterior Pressure

Paragraph one of chapter nine teaches us that man's will is free from any exterior pressure. The key word is absolute. Nothing from the outside can absolutely make us do something.

The confession says:

> God has endued the will of men with that natural liberty that is neither forced nor by any absolute necessity of nature determined to do good or evil.

What this tells us about the will itself, by creative design, is that there's nothing wrong with our will. It's not the will that needs to be changed. The will is like a machine—it works perfectly. Whatever raw material you put in will dictate what the output is. It's not the will that needs to be changed. Something else needs to be changing us—what pushes the will, what feeds the will. That's our nature, our heart.

The Lord Jesus speaks of this in Matthew 12:

> Neither make the tree good and its fruit good or else make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for a tree is known by its fruit. Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and an evil man out of the evil treasure brings forth evil things.

James says the same thing. It's not Satan who made me do it. My spouse did not make me do it. My kids did not make me do it. That's not why we sin.

James says:

> Each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desires.

It is not outside influences necessarily that absolutely make us sin. It's our nature pushing the will that the Lord has given us.

### Section Two: The Will Before the Fall

Paragraph two talks about the will of man before the fall. It says:

> Man in his state of innocence had freedom and power to will and to do that which was good and well pleasing to God, but yet mutably, so that he might fall from it.

Before the fall, man could do good and could do evil. He was able to please God. God made man upright, but it was a changeable will, a changeable nature, a changeable state. How do we know that state was changeable? It changed. We have the account in Genesis chapter three.

### Section Three: The Will After the Fall

Paragraph three talks about the will after the fall, the unregenerate will. It says:

> Man by his fall into a state of sin has wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation. So as a natural man being altogether averse from that good and dead in sin is not able by his own strength to convert himself or to prepare himself thereto.

The natural man after the fall cannot will salvation. Remember what Romans 5:6 says:

> When we were without strength, without the power to do so, Christ died for us.

But it's not just that he cannot. The natural man will not choose God because it's inconsistent with his nature. In Romans 3:10-12:

> As it is written, "There is none righteous, no, not one. There is none who understands. There is none who seeks God. No one, no natural man on his own is seeking God."

As a matter of fact, man is dead as far as choosing to believe in God through Jesus Christ. The apostle says in Ephesians 2:1:

> He made alive who are dead in your trespasses and sins.

This deadness makes it impossible for man to convert himself. Listen to First Corinthians 2:14:

> The natural man does not receive the things of the spirit of God, for they are foolish to him, nor can he know them because they are spiritually discerned.

The natural man apart from the work of the spirit will not come to God. It's not just that he cannot. He will not. He doesn't want to. And he does not have the ability to do so. That's the natural man—the will after the fall.

Historically, theologians have categorized this as the state of non posse peccare, non peccare—not able not to sin. A natural man is not able not to sin. Remember what the book of Proverbs says concerning the plowing of the wicked:

> The plowing of the wicked is an abomination before God.

Even just the common everyday activities of the wicked is an abomination before God because it's tainted with their own sin. They're not able not to sin.

### Section Four: The Will After Regeneration

We have the will of the converted man, the regenerate person. Paragraph four says:

> When God converts a sinner and translates him into the state of grace, he frees him from his natural bondage under sin and by his grace alone enables him freely to will and to do that which is spiritually good. Yet so as that by reason of his remaining corruption, he does not perfectly nor only will that which is good, but does also will that which is evil.

The saved person can choose to do good or can choose to obey God. He can also choose to disobey God. He's in the state of posse peccare, non posse peccare—able to sin, able not to sin.

Once a person is regenerate, the struggle is there, but it's the common experience of all believers. The presence of spiritual conflict is often evidence of spiritual life. The struggle is the evidence of the presence of the spirit. A lack of struggle is concerning.

What do I mean by struggle? Struggle means fighting, going against sin. Struggling doesn't mean doing it. The struggle is the fight, and the fight is the evidence of the presence of the spirit. Some of us have the spirit really present because the fight is gruesome and there all the time.

The unbeliever loves sin without conflict, but the believer increasingly hates sin even while battling it. So we are encouraged by this doctrine that even in our state of being regenerated by God, the struggle is there, but it's the common experience of all believers. That's how we become more like Jesus Christ.

### Section Five: The Will in Glory

And that brings us to the fifth section—men's will in glory when perfected. Paragraph five says:

> The will of man is made perfectly and immutably free to do good alone in the state of glory only.

Do you realize that this is a better state than Adam before the fall? Adam before the fall could sin and could not sin. That was his choice. But in eternity, we will not be able to sin. That's why the apostle John says:

> Behold, now we are children of God and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. But we know that when he has revealed, we shall be like him for we shall see him as he is.

We're going to be like Christ and not able to sin anymore. And that's the glory of heaven, which is greater than the glory of the garden. In eternity, we'll be in the state of non posse peccare—not able to sin anymore.

## Practical Applications

Why does this matter? What are the practical applications of this doctrine?

### First Application: Humility Before God

This doctrine should humble ourselves before God. If our wills are bound to our nature, then no one can boast that he chose Christ because he was wiser, more spiritual, or more virtuous than someone else. All of us were at some point in rebellion against God. We can't boast that Christ chose me or I came to Christ because I'm smarter or more intelligent, because we're all dead in our trespasses and our sins.

Salvation is entirely of grace. Every believer should be marked by humility rather than pride. We should regularly thank God for giving us a new heart that now enables our will to choose him.

### Second Application: Depend Completely Upon God's Grace

We should depend completely upon God's grace. Many people believe that they simply need to try harder to become a Christian or to please God or to be a better person. But this lesson reminds us that we do not merely need better habits. We need a new heart. It's not rearranging the furniture on the outside. That would be equivalent to rearranging the deck furniture on the Titanic as it's going down. It's pointless. Only the Holy Spirit can give spiritual life. This should make us rely upon God's grace every day instead of our own strength.

### Third Application: Pray Expectantly for the Salvation of Unbelievers

This doctrine should lead us to pray expectantly for the salvation of unbelievers. If conversion depended on human will alone, then we would have very little reason to pray. But because God changes hearts, we can pray confidently for unbelieving family members. We can pray for our children. We can pray for neighbors. We can pray for coworkers. We never give up on someone because no heart is too hard for God. This doctrine fuels evangelistic prayer rather than discourages it.

I'm always thankful to God that Christians are often inconsistent in their beliefs. You can be in a big argument with somebody who does not believe that God is sovereign in salvation, who thinks that people can choose God on their own. Yet when you get on your knees with them to pray for people, guess what they pray for? They pray that God would save those people. Because in what we pray and what we sing, a doctrine other than the sovereignty of God just doesn't lend itself to praying and singing.

### Fourth Application: Evangelize Faithfully

This doctrine also leads us to evangelize faithfully. Some object that God's sovereignty discourages evangelism, but the opposite is true. Since only God can change hearts, we pray, we proclaim Christ, we lovingly persuade sinners, and then we leave the result to God. This frees you to evangelism because the salvation of people is not on your shoulders. You're not in charge of saving that person. You can just present the gospel, be persuasive and winsome, and God is the one that does it. We don't have to worry about that.

Our confidence rests not in persuasive techniques, but in the power of the Holy Spirit. We are responsible for proclaiming the gospel, but we're not responsible for producing conversions. This was a big misunderstanding during the Second Great Awakening. Charles Finney, a Presbyterian minister, thought that he could psychologically create the environment that would produce true conversions. He believed it was completely up to the minister and to the church to create the conditions for true conversions, and that we did not need the Holy Spirit to do that. But that's not what the Bible teaches. Conversions are not up to us. Conversions are up to the Spirit. So we just proclaim the word.

### Fifth Application: Encouragement in Our Struggles

This lesson encourages us in our struggles. Many Christians become discouraged because they still battle sin. But paragraph four reminds us that we have a new nature, yet remaining corruption continues until glory. Our experience of struggle is not uncommon. Actually, that's the common experience of believers.

The presence of spiritual conflict is often evidence of spiritual life. The struggle is the evidence of the presence of the spirit. A lack of struggle is concerning. The struggle is the fight, and the fight is the evidence of the presence of the spirit. Some of us have the spirit really present because the fight is gruesome and there all the time.

The unbeliever loves sin without conflict, but the believer increasingly hates sin even while battling it. So we are encouraged by this doctrine that even in our state of being regenerated by God, the struggle is there, but it's the common experience of all believers, and that's how we become more like Jesus Christ.

## Greater Theological Implications

The doctrine of free will is not merely an abstract theological discussion. It teaches us that our greatest problem is not a lack of information, but a corrupt heart. And our greatest hope is not stronger determination but the sovereign grace of God.

Our society thinks, and this is a worldwide phenomenon, that education is the solution to all evils. If you can just educate people more, everything will be fixed. But the solution for all evils is the gospel of Jesus Christ because it's the heart that needs to be changed. The God who raised us from spiritual death continues to transform our hearts by his spirit. And one day he will perfect our wills in glory so that we will delight in him forever.

Are you looking forward to that? Until that day, let us humbly depend upon his grace, faithfully proclaim his gospel, diligently fight sin, and joyfully wait the day when we shall be like Christ. And that's going to be a glorious day.
